title: Early Childhood Education
summary: Learn to support young children's development: why the early years matter, learning through play, early literacy and numeracy, health and safety routines, observing and assessing children, and partnering with families.
audience: Pre-school and crèche practitioners, foundation-phase teachers, parents and education students

body.p: Early childhood education and care (ECEC) covers children from birth to about eight years, including crèches, playgroups, pre-schools and the first years of primary school. These years lay the foundations for health, learning and behaviour throughout life. Children who attend good-quality early learning programmes are generally better prepared for school, and the benefits are often largest for children from poorer families.

list: Physical: gross motor skills (running, climbing) and fine motor skills (holding a crayon, buttoning).
Cognitive: thinking, memory, problem-solving, early maths and science ideas.
Language and communication: listening, speaking, early reading and writing, often in more than one language.
Social and emotional: relationships, managing feelings, sharing and cooperation.
Creative: music, art, movement and imaginative play.

body.p: Development follows a broad sequence but at different speeds for each child. Milestones are guides, not deadlines; persistent delays should be discussed with families and, where needed, health or specialist services.

body.tip: Nurturing care (good health, nutrition, safety, responsive caregiving and early learning) works best when all parts are present together.

body.p: Play is how young children learn. Through play they explore, test ideas, use language, solve problems, cooperate and manage feelings. Adults guide play to extend learning without taking it over.

list: Free play: children choose what and how to play.
Guided play: the adult sets up materials or asks questions towards a learning goal, such as sorting bottle tops by colour and size.
Pretend play: shops, cooking or clinics, which build language and social skills.
Construction and manipulative play: blocks, clay, puzzles, sand and water.
Physical and outdoor play: running, climbing, ball games and traditional games and songs.
Prepare a safe, interesting environment with learning corners and low-cost or recycled materials.
Observe, then join in with open questions: "What will happen if…?" "How did you build it?"
Introduce new words and count, compare and describe during play.
Balance child-led and adult-led activities across the day.

body.tip: Collect free materials such as bottle tops, boxes, seeds and fabric scraps; they make excellent counting, sorting and building resources.

body.p: Strong language skills underpin later reading. Talk with children constantly, read aloud every day, sing songs and rhymes, and tell stories, including in the child's home language, which supports learning additional languages later.

list: Phonological awareness: hearing rhymes, syllables and the sounds in words.
Print awareness: books are read from front to back, text carries meaning.
Letter knowledge and early mark-making, from scribbles to letters.
Vocabulary: introduce rich words in context and repeat them.
Counting with one-to-one correspondence: touching each object once.
Comparing: more, fewer, longer, heavier.
Patterns and shapes: continue a bead pattern, find circles in the classroom.
Simple problems in everyday life: "There are 5 children and each needs 4 crayons. How many crayons do we need?" (20).

body.tip: Ask children to explain how they know; talking about thinking builds both language and reasoning.

body.p: Young children depend on adults for safety and health. Programmes need clear routines and policies.

list: Supervision: keep adult-to-child ratios that allow close supervision; these are set by national regulations and are lower for babies than for older children. For example, with a ratio of 1 adult to 10 children, 30 children need at least 3 adults; with 1 to 8, 26 children need at least 4.
Safe environment: cover sockets, store medicines and chemicals out of reach, check play equipment, supervise water.
Hygiene: hand washing with soap before eating and after toilet use; clean toilets and safe drinking water.
Nutrition: regular healthy meals and snacks; know children's allergies.
Health: check immunisation records, recognise signs of illness and have a plan for contacting parents and health services.
Child protection: know the signs of abuse and neglect and follow reporting procedures.

body.p: Routines (arrival, meals, rest, toileting and departure) are learning opportunities too: children practise independence, counting, conversation and cooperation.

body.tip: Keep emergency contacts, allergy information and a first-aid kit up to date and easy to find.

body.p: Assessment in the early years is mainly through observation during everyday activities, not tests. Observations show what each child can do, what they are ready to learn next and whether anyone needs extra support.

list: Anecdotal notes: brief, factual descriptions of what a child did and said.
Checklists of developmental skills.
Work samples: drawings, mark-making and photos of constructions, kept in a portfolio.
Time samples: noting what a child is doing every few minutes.

body.p: Record facts ("Amina counted 7 blocks correctly, touching each once") rather than judgements ("Amina is clever"). Use observations to plan activities and to talk with families. If an educator observes 5 children a day, every child in a class of 20 is observed at least once a week.

body.tip: Share positive observations with parents regularly, not only concerns; it builds the partnership you need when concerns do arise.

body.p: Families are children's first and most important teachers. Strong partnerships between educators and families improve children's learning and wellbeing.

list: Welcome families, learn about their culture, languages and routines, and show respect.
Communicate regularly through conversations at drop-off, messages, meetings and simple reports.
Suggest easy home activities: reading or telling stories, counting during cooking, singing songs.
Involve families in the programme as volunteers, storytellers or helpers.
Link families to community services such as clinics, social support and parenting programmes.

body.p: Every child has the right to take part, including children with disabilities, children from minority language groups and children affected by poverty or conflict. Adapt activities, materials and communication so all children can participate, and work with families and specialists to support children with additional needs.

body.tip: Ask families what their child enjoys at home; building on those interests makes children feel recognised and motivated.

quiz.q: Early childhood education usually covers children from birth to about:
Holding a crayon is an example of:
Developmental milestones should be treated as:
options: Broad guides, with persistent delays discussed

quiz.q: Sorting bottle tops by colour with an adult asking questions is:
Which question best extends a child's play?
options: What will happen if you add another block?

quiz.q: Reading aloud in the child's home language:
options: Supports later learning, including additional languages
